title: Personalized Multimodal Feedback Using Multiple External Representations: Strategy Profiles and Learning in High School Physics
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether personalized elaborated feedback delivered through multiple external representations (MERs) is associated with better learning outcomes in high school physics, and whether students differ in how they select and benefit from those representations. The authors frame the work in the context of adaptive learning, feedback, intelligent tutoring systems, and emerging multimodal large language models, arguing that systems should tailor not only feedback content but also the representational format used to explain physics concepts.

The study used a computer-based platform (KI4SCool) in which students first received verification feedback after each multiple-choice physics item and could optionally open elaborated feedback in three formats: verbal, graphical/pictorial, and mathematical. Data came from 661 high school students in Germany across 29 schools and 87 classes, followed over about 16 to 24 weeks during physics instruction on kinematics. The analysis was observational rather than experimental: the researchers modeled associations between feedback use and post-test performance, examined whether prior knowledge, confidence, and platform performance moderated these associations, and used clustering to identify recurring MER-selection strategies.

Results showed a small but consistent positive association between more frequent use of elaborated feedback and higher post-test scores, even after accounting for prior knowledge, platform performance, exercise count, and confidence. No robust evidence appeared for interactions with prior knowledge, platform score, or confidence. Clustering revealed several strategy profiles, including students who seldom opened elaborated feedback, students who mainly chose verbal feedback, students who distributed attention across formats, and students who often consulted all three representations together. The authors found no clear evidence that initial representational competence explained strategy choice, though one cluster suggested a stronger link between frequent feedback use and learning. They conclude that adaptive systems could benefit from tailoring feedback elaboration and representational format, while noting that the observational design prevents causal claims and that motivation could partly explain the associations.
quality_tier_rationale: This is an observational cohort study with clustering and covariate adjustment, not a randomized experiment. It provides useful evidence but leaves substantial room for confounding and self-selection, so credibility is moderate rather than high.
impact_tier_rationale: The observed associations are small and correlational, with no causal effect established. The work is informative for design, but the practical impact on learning remains modest and uncertain.

interventions.use_case: computer-based physics practice platform providing immediate verification feedback plus optional elaborated feedback in verbal, graphical, and mathematical formats
proposed adaptive feedback design for an ITS that tailors feedback elaboration and representational format to learner profiles

finding.finding_summary: In this prospective observational study of high school physics (n=661), greater use of elaborated multirepresentational feedback was associated with higher post-test physics scores after adjusting for pre-test performance, platform score, exercises solved, and confidence. The adjusted association was small but consistent across cohorts (Cohort 1 standardized β=0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22]; Cohort 2 β=0.08, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16], p=.054).
finding.measure: Post-test physics score (%) from kinematics assessments

finding.finding_summary: Feedback frequency was not meaningfully related to prior knowledge, platform score, number of exercises solved, or average confidence, suggesting the observed association was not simply explained by these measured learner characteristics. The only notable correlation was with average response time (r=.43 in Cohort 1; r=.34 in Cohort 2), indicating a modest link between time spent thinking and feedback use rather than a broad motivational profile.
finding.measure: Pearson correlations between feedback frequency and response time, pre-test score, platform score, exercises solved, and average confidence
finding.effect_size: r=.43 (response time, Cohort 1); r=.34 (response time, Cohort 2)
